We also observe that UPLC does not capture the full strength of the non-adaptive iterative pigeonhole principle. We define a new problem T-UPLC (Definition VI.17), which is similar to UPLC, but has the strongest possible parameters. We show that T-UPLC is indeed PAP-complete (Lemma VI.18), therefore, the non-adaptive iterative pigeonhole principle is equivalent to the generalized pigeonhole principle. Taken together, our results provide a nearly complete picture (see Figure 1 for a summary) of the relative complexities of the Pecking Order, PLC, UPLC, R AMSEY, and B I R AMSEY in the black-box setting. 4) PLS, PPA, and the Pecking Order: Given these results, it is also quite natural to try and relate the Pecking Order classes to other well-studied and important TFNP subclasses. We focus on the relationships with the classes PLS and PPA, which are the two of the three strongest TFNP subclasses out of the “original five” TFNP subclasses defined by Papadimitriou [2] (the third being PPP). The seminal work of Beame et. al. [3] has shown that the important TFNP subclass PPA, embodying the Handshaking Lemma, is not contained in PPP in the black-box setting. The recent breakthrough of [16] showed that the TFNP subclass PLS, embodying problems with (not necessarily efficient) local search heuristics, is also not contained in PPP in the black-box setting. Using our techniques, we improve these results, showing that neither of these classes are even contained in PAP — the highest level of the Pecking Order: Theorem I.14.
